title: Leiden Censure: present-tense remitting fiducia justifies — past-tense follows
source_text: LXIV. Haec est quoque doctrina Professorum Leydensium, in Censura capitis undecimi Confessionis Remonstrantium, cujus author Andreas Rivetus. Non dicimus, inquiunt, fiduciam illam qua justificamur, esse remissionis peccatorum jam perceptae, vel objectum illius fiduciae esse remissionem peccatorum antea perceptam: sed fiduciam illam qua credimus quisque, nobis remitti peccata in praesenti, non proprie in praeterito, nec in futuro, etsi etiam utrumque ad fidem justificantem pertineat, sed non ad justificandi actum, ut ita dicam, formalem. Dum ergo per verbum Evangelii offertur a Deo cuilibet credenti misericordia & remissio peccatorum per Christum, non solum fides credit in genere hoc verum esse, remissum iri nempe peccata omnibus vere in Christum credentibus, sed etiam hic sibi fidenter persuadet qui credit, promissionem illam ad se pertinere, & illo fiduciae actu recipi; proinde ipsi tum remitti peccatum, suam esse beatitudinem illam de qua Apostolus ad Romanos 4. vers. 7. Quomodo extensa manu, & accepto munere, fit beneficii particeps, qui veniam accesserat. Itaque simul sunt remissio peccatorum, & fiducia de eadem remissione in homine fideli; & ut fide recepta est misericordia illa, & gratia specialis, eadem posita retinentur; & quae de futuro credebatur, in praesenti annexa est, de praeterito posita certa manet. Sed qui credit se justificatum iri, si credat in Jesum Christum, nondum eatenus justificatus est; nisi etiam & in praesenti credat sibi justitiam dari, quam eodem actu accipiat. Quod autem postea credit de praeterito, non eum justificat, sed supponit justificatum. Sunt autem omnes illi actus unius & ejusdem fidei justificantis, primus quidem ad justificationem disponens, secundus proprie justificans, tertius conscientiam pacificans.
pass_a_gloss: This is also the doctrine of the Leiden Professors in the Censure of the eleventh chapter of the Remonstrant Confession, whose author is Andreas Rivetus. We do not say, they say, that that trust by which we are justified is of remission of sins already perceived, or that the object of that trust is remission of sins previously perceived: but that trust by which each of us believes that sins are remitted to us in the present — not properly in the past, nor in the future — although both also pertain to justifying faith, yet not to the formal act of justifying, so to speak. While therefore through the word of the Gospel mercy and remission of sins through Christ are offered by God to every believer, faith not only believes in general that this is true — namely that sins will be remitted to all who truly believe in Christ — but also here he who believes confidently persuades himself that that promise pertains to him, and is received by that act of trust; and therefore that sin is then remitted to him, that that blessedness of which the Apostle speaks to the Romans 4:7 is his. As by an extended hand, and a gift received, he becomes partaker of the benefit who had come for pardon. And so remission of sins and trust concerning the same remission are simultaneous in the faithful man; and as that mercy and special grace were received by faith, the same once given are retained; and what was believed concerning the future is annexed in the present, and concerning the past, once given, remains sure. But he who believes that he will be justified if he believes in Jesus Christ is not yet justified so far; unless he also in the present believes that justice is given to him, which he receives by the same act. But what he afterward believes concerning the past does not justify him, but presupposes him justified. And all those acts are of one and the same justifying faith — the first indeed disposing to justification, the second properly justifying, the third pacifying the conscience.
pass_b_english: Leiden Censure (Rivetus): justifying fiducia ≠ already-perceived remission.
Formal act: believe sins are remitted to me now (present), not past/future as such.
General truth + personal ‘this promise is mine and received’ — then remission and fiducia are simultaneous.
‘I will be justified if I believe’ alone does not justify — need present reception of justice.
One faith, three acts: disposing / properly justifying / conscience-pacifying.
